title: No fixed mind
hookLine: the sage has no fixed mind and is good even to those who are not good (Tao Te Ching 49)

lines: SOMEONE WHO DOESN'T KEEP THE RULE.
cards: The neighbor who never waves back. The relative who turns every holiday into a debate. The driver who cuts across two lanes and then glares at you.
A quiet rule runs under a lot of daily life: be good to people who are good to you, and give the others what they give. It feels fair.
Chapter forty-nine of the Tao Te Ching describes someone who doesn't keep that rule, and starts by saying this person has no fixed mind.

teach.h: NO INVARIABLE MIND OF HIS OWN.
teach.b: First, the opening. In James Legge's translation: "The sage has no invariable mind of his own; he makes the mind of the people his mind." No fixed mind doesn't mean no opinions.
It means not walking in with a verdict already decided, and letting other people's lives and needs shape how you see. Second, the hard line.

teach.h: GOOD TO THOSE WHO ARE NOT GOOD.
teach.b: Legge again: "To those who are good (to me), I am good; and to those who are not good (to me), I am also good." The same goes for trust: the sage is sincere with the sincere, and with the insincere too.
The reason given is that goodness spreads this way. Kindness that waits for kindness first is a trade. Kindness given anyway changes what happens next.

teach.h: NOT A DUTY TO STAY IN HARM'S WAY.
teach.b: The chapter describes a way of meeting people, not a duty to stay in harm's way. Being good to someone can mean a calm word, a fair deal, or a door held open, while still keeping a safe distance.
Good to all is about the heart you bring, not about letting anyone hurt you.
If someone is hurting you, your safety comes first: in the US you can call or text 988 at any hour, and wherever you are, local emergency help is there. Fourth, the ending.
The sage treats people the way a parent treats children. Children aren't kind every minute either, and a parent doesn't reset the whole relationship after one rude remark.
Chapter forty-nine asks for that steadiness with the neighbor, the relative, the driver.
Not a fixed mind. An open one.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter forty-nine as a model for meeting difficult people with steady goodwill, without first deciding who they are, while still keeping themselves safe.

o: not walking in with a verdict already decided
having no opinions or beliefs of your own
changing your mind to please whoever's near

p: has no invariable mind of his own
the sage is good to them too
the sage is sincere with them too

s: no fixed mind means having no opinions
it means not walking in with a verdict, and making the people's mind your mind.
the chapter treats sincerity the same way as goodness
sincere with the sincere, and with the insincere too.
chapter forty-nine says to stay near anyone who harms you
it describes a way of meeting people, not a duty to stay in harm's way.

games.q: a neighbor ignores your wave, again. what does chapter forty-nine's sage do?
o: stop waving; give what you get.
games.why: the chapter says the sage is good to those who are good, and also good to those who are not, and that goodness spreads this way.

practice: Let one person come to mind who hasn't been good to you lately, someone you can safely think about, and notice the verdict you've already reached about them. Set it down, just for these two minutes.
If you pray, you might hold them in your prayer; if you don't, wish them one simple good thing: rest, a better day, a kind word from someone.

carryVoice: Your line: good to all. Steady, the way a parent stays steady. See you tomorrow.
